Since $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(\alpha,\beta)} \in R$ and $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(\beta,\delta)} \in R,$ but $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(\alpha,\delta)} \notin R,$ the relation is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{not transitive}}.$

It's sufficient to check all the "linked" pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x \neq y$ and $(y,z)$ with $y \neq z.$

For our relation, notice that

  • $(3,5) \in R$ since $3 \not\mid 5,$ and

  • $(5,6) \in R$ since $5 \not\mid 6,$ but

  • $(3,6) \notin R$ since $3 \mid 6.$

Therefore, we can conclude the following:

Since $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(3,5) \in R}$ and $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(5,6) \in R}$ but $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}(3,6) \notin R},$ the relation is $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{not transitive}}.$

question.text:
Which of the following relations are transitive?

  • $x \: R \: y$ if and only if $x+y < 0,$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$

  • $x \: S \: y$ if and only if $x+y=2,$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$

  • $x \: T \: y$ if and only if $x \equiv y+1 \:(\text{mod}\:3),$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}$
question.explanation:
A binary relation $R$ defined on a set $A$ is transitive if, for all $x,y,z \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,z) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,z) \in R. \] In other words, if the pairs $(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$ belong to a transitive relation, then the pair $(x,z)$ should also be in the relation.

It's sufficient to check all the "linked" pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x \neq y$ and $(y,z)$ with $y \neq z.$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • Relation $R$ is not transitive. Notice that

    • $(-4,-6) \in R$ since $-4+ (-6)= -10 < 0,$ and

    • $(-6,5) \in R$ since $-6 + 5=-1 < 0,$ but

    • $(-4,5) \notin R$ since $-4 + 5 = 1 \not\lt 0.$

  • Relation $S$ is not transitive. Notice that

    • $(-2,4) \in S$ since $-2+ 4= 2,$ and

    • $(4,-2) \in S$ since $4 + (-2)= 2,$ but

    • $(-2,-2) \notin S$ since $ -2+ (-2) = -4 \neq 2.$

  • Relation $T$ is not transitive. Notice that

    • $(0, 2 ) \in T$ since $0 \equiv 2+1 \:(\text{mod}\:3),$ and

    • $(2, 4) \in T$ since $2 \equiv 4+1 \:(\text{mod}\:3),$ but

    • $(0,4) \notin T$ since $ 0 \not\equiv 4+1 \:(\text{mod}\:3).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None."

example.title: Transitive Relations Defined On Infinite Sets

question.text:
Which of the following relations are transitive?

  • $x \: R \: y$ if and only if $x-y \gt -5,$ defined on $\mathbb{Q}$

  • $x \: S \: y$ if and only if $xy < 0,$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$

  • $x \: T \: y$ if and only if $x \gt y,$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}$
question.explanation:
A binary relation $R$ defined on a set $A$ is transitive if, for all $x,y,z \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,z) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad (x,z) \in R. \] In other words, if the pairs $(x,y)$ and $(y,z)$ belong to a transitive relation, then the pair $(x,z)$ should also be in the relation.

It's sufficient to check all the "linked" pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x \neq y$ and $(y,z)$ with $y \neq z.$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • Relation $R$ is not transitive. Notice that

    • $(1,5) \in R$ since $1-5=-4 \gt -5,$ and

    • $(5,9) \in R$ since $5-9=-4 \gt -5,$ but

    • $(1,9) \notin R$ since $1-9=-8 \not\gt -5.$

  • Relation $S$ is not transitive. Notice that

    • $(-1,2) \in S$ since $(-1) \cdot 2 = -2 \lt 0,$ and

    • $(2,-3) \in S$ since $2 \cdot (-3) = -6 \lt 0,$ but

    • $(-1,-3) \notin S$ since $(-1) \cdot (-3) = 3 \not\lt 0.$

  • Relation $T$ is transitive. Indeed, if $(x,y) \in R$ and $(y,x) \in R,$ then $(x,z) \in R.$ Notice that \[ x \gt y \quad\textrm{and}\quad y \gt z \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x \gt z \] for all $x,y,z \in \mathbb{Z}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$T$ only."
